appraisal_events.evidence: «des reproches qui me semblèrent du reste fort justes, et auxquels Saint-Loup, tout en désobéissant à Rachel sur l'article du champagne, adhéra entièrement»; «sentais la bonne influence de sa maîtresse, j'étais tout prêt à lui conseiller d'envoyer promener sa famille»
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly ratifies Rachel's judgment as just and credits her with a good influence over Saint-Loup, who assents entirely; her verdict on the family carries the room, giving her the dominant moral and rhetorical authority in the scene.

appraisal_events.evidence: «croyez-vous que la mère de Robert, une femme pieuse, dit qu'il faut qu'il reste à l'île du Diable, même s'il est innocent ? n'est-ce pas une horreur ?»
appraisal_events.explanation: Rachel, weeping over Dreyfus as a martyr, sets Saint-Loup's pious mother's willingness to keep an innocent man on Devil's Island against her professed piety; the charge extends the reproaches the narrator has just called fort justes and goes uncontradicted.

status_effects.explanation: She speaks with authority that both the narrator and Saint-Loup accept, and her indignant rhetorical question closes the passage unanswered.
The narrator presents her as a just and salutary influence, and her Dreyfusard grief reads as moral credit within the local scene.
She is locally condemned as a hypocrite whose piety coexists with wanting an innocent man to die in penal exile.
He yields to his mistress, adhering entirely to her attack on his own family and disobeying her only over champagne, so leverage in the scene lies with her.
He is locally elevated as an innocent martyr whose children will bear an unstained name, with Saint-Loup and the narrator offering no dissent.

ambiguities: The parenthetical «car elle prenait au sérieux l'art dramatique» is a narratorial aside that can be read as dry irony at Rachel's expense; it qualifies the tone of her elevation without reversing the explicit endorsement of her reproaches as «fort justes».

Mme de Marsantes' position on Dreyfus is reported at second hand by Rachel, an interested party in the quarrel with Saint-Loup's family, so her local diminishment rests on unverified hearsay that the narrator does not directly confirm.
